NiftyQuant Analytics: Momentum, Risk and the Shapes of Indian Stocks¶

FDS course project (NiftyQuant). The database holds every NSE cash-market trade summary from January 2010 to October 2026: 7.3 million daily prices for 3,865 securities, adjusted for 1,500 splits, bonuses and rights issues parsed from NSE's own corporate-action feed, in a BCNF schema whose triggers stop look-ahead bias getting into the backtest. This notebook asks:

  1. How do Indian stock returns behave? Fat tails, liquidity, risk by sector.
  2. Does momentum work in India, and when does it fail?
  3. What kinds of stocks are there? k-means on risk/return behaviour, and which kind protects you when the market falls.

Workflow

  1. SQL first. Statistics run inside PostgreSQL (07_analytics.sql, A1–A5, and the backtest views of 03_logic.sql). Only aggregates leave the database.
  2. Statistical tests on those aggregates (t-tests, bootstrap, χ²).
  3. Feature engineering in SQL. v_stock_features turns 60 months of prices into one row per stock in today's universe.
  4. k-means on standardized features; k chosen by elbow, silhouette and interpretability.
  5. Write back the labels to the BCNF tables segment / security_segment, then answer S1–S2 in SQL.

Data: NSE India bhavcopy and corporate-action archives; index levels from Yahoo Finance. Research use only; not investment advice.

0. Setup¶

Reads use the role niftyquant_readonly (SELECT only). Only the write-back in §5 connects as the owner: least privilege. run_sql() runs one labelled query from 07_analytics.sql, so the SQL on the slides and the SQL executed here are the same text.

In [1]:
import os
import re
import warnings

os.environ.setdefault("LOKY_MAX_CPU_COUNT", "4")   # stops joblib probing the CPU count on Windows
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)
pd.set_option("display.width", 160)

OPTS = {"options": "-c search_path=niftyquant,public"}
reader = create_engine("postgresql+psycopg://niftyquant_readonly:readonly@localhost/niftyquant", connect_args=OPTS)
writer = create_engine("postgresql+psycopg://postgres:postgres@localhost/niftyquant", connect_args=OPTS)

ROOT = Path.cwd() if (Path.cwd() / "07_analytics.sql").exists() else Path.cwd().parent
SQL_FILE = ROOT / "07_analytics.sql"
FIG = ROOT / "analytics" / "figures"
FIG.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# A labelled query in 07_analytics.sql is a "-- A1. TITLE" header block,
# closed by a "-- ====" line, followed by one statement ending in ";".
_QUERY = re.compile(r"^-- ([AS]\d)\. ([^\n]*)\n.*?^-- =+\n\n(.*?;)\s*$", re.M | re.S)
QUERIES = {m[1]: (m[2].strip(), m[3]) for m in _QUERY.finditer(SQL_FILE.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))}

def run_sql(label):
    title, sql = QUERIES[label]
    print(f"{label}. {title}")
    return num(query(sql))

def query(sql, **params):
    with reader.connect() as c:
        return pd.read_sql(text(sql), c, params=params)

def num(df):
    """NUMERIC columns arrive as Decimal objects: make them floats."""
    for c in df.columns:
        if df[c].dtype == object:
            try:
                df[c] = pd.to_numeric(df[c])
            except (ValueError, TypeError):
                pass
    return df

def month_label(n):
    """month_no (year*12 + month) -> Timestamp of that month's first day."""
    n = int(n)
    return pd.Timestamp(year=(n - 1) // 12, month=(n - 1) % 12 + 1, day=1)

print("Queries found:", ", ".join(QUERIES))

Queries found: A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6, A7, S1, S2

n = 97,963; Jarque-Bera = 214,303, p = 0.0e+00

Reading A1. Monthly returns are far from normal. Across 97,963 stock-months the excess kurtosis is 7.0 (a normal has 0) and the skew is +0.86: most months are quiet, a few are enormous, and the big ones are more often up than down for single stocks (the 99th percentile is +41%, the 1st is −31%). The index is different: its skew is −0.58, because diversification cancels the single-stock jumps, but crashes hit everything at once. Jarque–Bera rejects normality outright. This is why §2 backs the t-test with a bootstrap.

Reading A5. There is only a weak liquidity premium. The least traded fifth of the universe (ranks 401–500, about ₹12 crore a day) earned 1.20% a month on average, against 0.84% for the 100 most traded (about ₹268 crore a day), with more volatility (14.0% against 11.6% a month). The ordering is not monotonic (ranks 301–400 earned less than 201–300), so liquidity alone is not a strategy, but it is a reason the momentum test equal-weights within one universe instead of comparing stocks of very different sizes.

Reading A4. The median NIFTY 500 stock has a beta of 1.14: an equal-weighted universe is riskier than the cap-weighted index. Construction (1.63), Realty (1.58) and Power (1.55) amplify the market most; Healthcare (0.87), FMCG (0.92) and IT (0.98) damp it, as finance textbooks predict for non-cyclical demand. The average R² is only about 0.25: three-quarters of a typical stock's monthly movement is its own, not the market's.

2. Does momentum work in India?¶

The backtest is built in SQL (03_logic.sql): at every month-end, the 500 most liquid shares as known that day are ranked on their return over the past 12 months excluding the latest one (12-1 momentum), split into deciles, and held for the next month, equally weighted. Triggers and a composite FK make it impossible for a holding to be a stock that was not in that day's universe (no look-ahead).

2.1 The decile scorecard¶

In [9]:
dec = num(query("""
    SELECT r.bucket, r.holding_month_no, r.ret
    FROM v_portfolio_return r JOIN strategy s USING (strategy_id)
    WHERE s.strategy_code = 'MOM_12_1'"""))
idx = num(query("SELECT month_no AS holding_month_no, ret AS nifty FROM v_index_monthly_return WHERE index_code = 'NIFTY500'"))
wide = dec.pivot(index="holding_month_no", columns="bucket", values="ret").merge(idx, on="holding_month_no").set_index("holding_month_no")
wide["WML"] = wide[10] - wide[1]

def scorecard(s):
    s = s.dropna()
    w = (1 + s).cumprod()
    return pd.Series({"months": len(s), "CAGR %": 100 * (w.iloc[-1] ** (12 / len(s)) - 1),
                      "vol %": 100 * s.std() * np.sqrt(12), "Sharpe (rf=0)": s.mean() / s.std() * np.sqrt(12),
                      "max DD %": 100 * (w / w.cummax() - 1).min()})
cols = list(range(1, 11)) + ["WML", "nifty"]
sc = pd.DataFrame({c: scorecard(wide[c]) for c in cols}).T.round(2)
sc.index = [f"D{c:02d}" if isinstance(c, int) else ("NIFTY 500" if c == "nifty" else "WML (D10-D01)") for c in cols]
sc

Is the winners-minus-losers premium distinguishable from zero? A t-test assumes monthly returns are independent and roughly normal (A1 says they're not normal), so we also bootstrap the mean: resample the months 10,000 times.

In [11]:
w = wide["WML"].dropna()
t, p = stats.ttest_1samp(w, 0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
boot = rng.choice(w.values, size=(10_000, len(w)), replace=True).mean(axis=1)
lo, hi = np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f"WML: mean {100 * w.mean():.2f}% a month over {len(w)} months; t = {t:.2f}, p = {p:.1e}")
print(f"Bootstrap 95% CI for the monthly mean: [{100 * lo:.2f}%, {100 * hi:.2f}%]")

WML: mean 2.34% a month over 190 months; t = 4.52, p = 1.1e-05
Bootstrap 95% CI for the monthly mean: [1.30%, 3.34%]

Reading 2.1. Momentum works in India, strongly. Over 190 holding months (Jan 2011 – Oct 2026; October is partial), return rises almost steadily with last year's return: the losers decile compounded at −7.0% a year, the winners at +26.3%, against 9.9% for the NIFTY 500. Winners-minus-losers earned 2.34% a month (t = 4.52; bootstrap 95% CI 1.30%–3.34%), positive in 72% of months. The winners also had a better Sharpe ratio than the index (1.02 against 0.64) and a smaller worst drawdown than the losers (−41% against −88%).

The effect is robust to the look-back but weaker among large caps: winners-minus-losers compounded at 27.9% a year (Sharpe 1.13) for 12-1 deciles of the top 500, 23.6% (1.09) for 6-1, and 13.0% (0.67) for 12-1 quintiles of the 200 most liquid stocks. Momentum is strongest where information spreads slowest.

Three honest caveats. These are gross, price-only, equal-weighted returns; Q3 in 05_queries.sql shows that a 0.5% cost per rebalance on ~27% monthly turnover cuts ₹1 lakh's final value from ₹40.5 lakh to ₹31.2 lakh (still against ₹4.4 lakh in the index). Holdings that stopped trading in the holding month are dropped, but that is 0.05% of holdings. And a 16-year sample contains only a handful of momentum crashes (A3).

months mean_ic sd_ic t_stat pct_months_positive
0 190 0.06 0.168 4.9 66.0

Reading A2. The 12-1 signal ranks next month's returns better than chance in two months out of three. The average rank correlation (IC) is 0.06, which sounds small, but it is persistent: t = 4.9 over 190 months. Quant managers treat an IC of 0.05 as useful because it applies to 500 stocks at once, every month.

Reading A3. Momentum crashes have one shape: a sharp market rebound after a fall. The worst month, June 2020 (−33.6%), came when the NIFTY 500 was up 8% after a 12-month fall of 20%: last year's losers jumped 41%. April 2020 and January 2012 look the same. May 2014 (election result) is the exception that proves the rule: a sudden re-rating where beaten-down cyclicals rallied 27%. Momentum is a bet that trends continue, and it loses when the trend snaps upward.

2.2 Survivorship bias, measured (query Q2 of 05_queries.sql)¶

The same universe, restricted to the stocks still listed today, is what a backtest built from today's index list would see.

In [15]:
q2 = num(query("""
WITH survivor AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT p.security_id FROM daily_price p
    WHERE p.trade_date >= (SELECT min(trade_date) FROM (SELECT trade_date FROM trading_day
                                                         ORDER BY trade_date DESC LIMIT 10) t)
), monthly AS (
    SELECT u.month_end, avg(m.ret) AS all_members,
           avg(m.ret) FILTER (WHERE s.security_id IS NOT NULL) AS survivors_only
    FROM universe_member u
    JOIN mv_monthly_return m ON m.security_id = u.security_id AND m.month_no = month_no(u.month_end) + 1
    LEFT JOIN survivor s ON s.security_id = u.security_id
    GROUP BY u.month_end)
SELECT * FROM monthly ORDER BY month_end"""))
g = (1 + q2[["all_members", "survivors_only"]]).cumprod()
yrs = len(q2) / 12
cagr = 100 * (g.iloc[-1] ** (1 / yrs) - 1)
print(f"Equal-weighted universe CAGR {cagr.all_members:.1f}%   survivors only {cagr.survivors_only:.1f}%"
      f"   -> bias {cagr.survivors_only - cagr.all_members:.1f} points a year")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.2))
ax.plot(q2.month_end, g.survivors_only, color=ORANGE, lw=1.8, label="Survivors only (what today's list shows)")
ax.plot(q2.month_end, g.all_members, color=BLUE, lw=1.8, label="Point-in-time universe (what was investable)")
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_ylabel("Growth of ₹1 (log)"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Survivorship bias: the gap is the stocks that later disappeared")
save(fig, "05_survivorship"); plt.show()

Equal-weighted universe CAGR 10.1%   survivors only 12.4%   -> bias 2.4 points a year

Reading 2.2. Survivorship bias is real and large. Restricting the same universe to stocks still listed today raises its equal-weighted return from 10.1% to 12.4% a year: 2.4 points a year of returns that never existed. The gap is widest in 2012–2014 (5–7 points a year, Q2), when an average of 94–123 of each month's 500 members later delisted, and it shrinks towards zero for recent years only because recent members haven't yet had time to fail. This is why the universe is rebuilt at every month-end from the prices known that day, with delisted stocks included.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.4))
sig = a6.t_stat >= 1.96
ax.bar(a6.months_after_formation, a6.wml_pct, color=[BLUE if s else MID for s in sig], edgecolor=GRID)
ax.set_xlabel("Months after the portfolio is formed"); ax.set_ylabel("Winners minus losers, % in that month")
ax.set_xticks(range(1, 13)); ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax2 = ax.twinx(); ax2.plot(a6.months_after_formation, a6.cumulative_pct, color=ORANGE, marker="o", lw=2)
ax2.set_ylabel("Running total, %"); ax2.grid(False); ax2.spines["right"].set_visible(True); ax2.set_ylim(0, None)
ax.set_title("The premium fades over a year but never reverses (blue: t ≥ 1.96)")
save(fig, "11_horizon_decay"); plt.show()

Reading A6. Momentum is slow, not a flash. The premium is largest in the first month (2.34%) and fades steadily, but stays significant in 10 of the 12 months and never turns negative: holding the same portfolio for a year adds up to about 15%. There is no reversal, so this is not traders overshooting and then correcting. It fits the slow-diffusion explanation: news about a company reaches its price over months, not days. The practical consequence is that monthly rebalancing is not essential; a slower strategy keeps most of the premium with far less trading.

Reading A7. This is the most important result in the project. Momentum works only after the market has risen. In the 144 months that followed a rising year for the NIFTY 500, winners-minus-losers earned 3.13% a month (t = 6.3). In the 45 months that followed a falling year it earned −0.30% (t = −0.2): nothing. The cause is visible in the two legs. After a falling year, last year's losers (the stocks that fell hardest) bounce back by 3.65% a month, more than the winners' 3.35%. A bear market ends with a rebound led by the most beaten-down stocks, and that is exactly where a momentum strategy is short.

Is momentum just market risk? (CAPM regression)¶

Each portfolio's monthly return regressed on the NIFTY 500's: the intercept (α) is the return the market does not explain, the slope (β) its market exposure.

In [20]:
rows = []
for name, col in [("Winners (D10)", 10), ("Losers (D01)", 1), ("Winners minus losers", "WML")]:
    s = wide[[col, "nifty"]].dropna()
    r = stats.linregress(s["nifty"], s[col])
    rows.append((name, 100 * r.intercept, r.intercept / r.intercept_stderr, r.slope, r.rvalue ** 2))
capm = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["portfolio", "alpha % a month", "alpha t", "beta", "R²"]).round(2)
capm
Out[20]:
portfolio alpha % a month alpha t beta R²
0 Winners (D10) 1.14 3.27 1.24 0.63
1 Losers (D01) -1.66 -3.87 1.75 0.69
2 Winners minus losers 2.80 5.67 -0.51 0.12

Reading the regression. Momentum is not compensation for market risk. Winners-minus-losers has a negative beta (−0.51): losers are more sensitive to the market (β 1.75) than winners (β 1.24), because last year's losers are mostly high-risk stocks. Yet its alpha is 2.80% a month (t = 5.7). Both legs contribute: winners beat their market exposure by 1.14% a month, losers fall short by 1.66%. The negative beta also explains A7: when the market rebounds sharply, a negative-beta portfolio loses.

Has it faded? Sub-periods¶

In [21]:
yr = pd.Series([(n - 1) // 12 for n in wide.index], index=wide.index)
rows = []
for a, b in [(2011, 2015), (2016, 2019), (2020, 2026)]:
    s = wide.loc[(yr >= a) & (yr <= b), "WML"].dropna()
    rows.append((f"{a}-{b}", len(s), 100 * s.mean(), s.mean() / s.std() * np.sqrt(len(s)), s.mean() / s.std() * np.sqrt(12)))
sub = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["period", "months", "WML % a month", "t", "Sharpe"]).round(2)
sub
Out[21]:
period months WML % a month t Sharpe
0 2011-2015 60 2.99 2.98 1.33
1 2016-2019 48 2.46 2.79 1.39
2 2020-2026 82 1.78 2.23 0.85

Reading the sub-periods. The premium is shrinking. It fell from 2.99% a month (2011–15) to 2.46% (2016–19) to 1.78% (2020–26), and the Sharpe ratio from about 1.4 to 0.85. It is still significant in every period (t ≥ 2.2). A falling premium is what finance expects once an anomaly is widely known and traded; we did not test the cause, and the 2020–26 period also contains the largest crash (June 2020).

Can the crashes be avoided?¶

Two ways to manage the risk, both using only information available at formation:

  • Volatility scaling: size the long-short position to target 20% annual volatility, using the standard deviation of its previous 12 monthly returns (leverage capped at 2×).
  • Market-state rule (from A7): hold winners-minus-losers only after a rising year for the NIFTY 500; otherwise stay in cash.
In [22]:
nifty_all = idx.set_index("holding_month_no")["nifty"].sort_index()
prior = np.log1p(nifty_all).rolling(12).sum().shift(1).reindex(wide.index)
wml = wide["WML"]
vol = wml.rolling(12).std().shift(1) * np.sqrt(12)
scaled = wml * (0.20 / vol).clip(upper=2)
timed = wml.where(prior >= 0, 0.0)
variants = {"Always on": wml, "Volatility-scaled": scaled, "Only after a rising year": timed}
common = scaled.dropna().index
tab = pd.DataFrame({k: scorecard(v.loc[common]) for k, v in variants.items()}).T
tab["worst month %"] = [100 * v.loc[common].min() for v in variants.values()]
tab = tab.round(2); tab

months CAGR % vol % Sharpe (rf=0) max DD % worst month %

Volatility-scaled 178.0 24.53 24.11 1.04 -34.71 -33.99

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.4))
dts = [month_label(n) for n in common]
for (k, v), c in zip(variants.items(), [MID, ORANGE, BLUE]):
    ax.plot(dts, (1 + v.loc[common]).cumprod(), lw=2 if c == BLUE else 1.6, color=INK2 if c == MID else c, label=k)
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_ylabel("Growth of ₹1, long-short (log)"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Sitting out after falling years removes the worst crashes")
save(fig, "13_crash_control"); plt.show()

Reading the comparison. Scaling by recent volatility barely helps: the Sharpe ratio moves from 1.01 to 1.04 and the worst drawdown improves (−48% to −35%), but the worst month is unchanged (−34%), because June 2020's crash came after a calm period. The rule from A7, staying in cash after a falling year, does what volatility scaling cannot: Sharpe 1.47, worst drawdown −32%, worst month −18%, and a higher return (29.3% against 24.4% a year), because the months it skips earned nothing on average.

One caution decides how far to trust this. The rule uses only information available at each formation date, so it is not look-ahead. But we chose it after seeing A7 on the same data, so 1.47 is an in-sample figure. The same market-state effect is documented for US stocks (Cooper, Gutierrez and Hameed, "Market States and Momentum", Journal of Finance, 2004), which makes it more than a fitted accident, but it needs an out-of-sample test before anyone trades it. (Both comparisons use the 178 months where 12 months of history exist for the volatility estimate.)

How much trading cost can it absorb? Does skipping the last month matter?¶

In [24]:
held = num(query("""SELECT month_no(h.formation_date) AS fm, h.security_id
                    FROM portfolio_holding h JOIN strategy s USING (strategy_id)
                    WHERE s.strategy_code = 'MOM_12_1' AND h.bucket = 10"""))
sets = held.groupby("fm").security_id.apply(set)
turn = pd.Series({fm + 1: (len(s - sets.get(fm - 1, set())) / len(s)) if (fm - 1) in sets.index else 1.0
                  for fm, s in sets.items()}).reindex(wide.index).fillna(1.0)
index_final = (1 + wide["nifty"]).prod()
lo, hi = 0.0, 0.2
for _ in range(60):          # bisection: the cost per unit traded at which winners = index
    mid = (lo + hi) / 2
    lo, hi = (mid, hi) if ((1 + wide[10]) * (1 - mid * turn)).prod() > index_final else (lo, mid)
print(f"Average monthly turnover of the winners decile: {100 * turn.mean():.1f}%")
print(f"Break-even cost: {100 * lo:.2f}% of the value traded at each rebalance")

mret = num(query("SELECT security_id, month_no, ret FROM mv_monthly_return"))
univ = num(query("SELECT month_no(month_end) AS fm, security_id FROM universe_member"))
W = mret.pivot(index="month_no", columns="security_id", values="ret"); LW = np.log1p(W)
signals = {"12-0 (includes the last month)": LW.rolling(12, min_periods=12).sum(),
           "12-1 (skips it)": LW.shift(1).rolling(11, min_periods=11).sum(),
           "1-0 (last month only)": LW}
rows = []
for name, S in signals.items():
    x = univ.copy()
    x["sig"] = S.stack().reindex(pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([x.fm, x.security_id])).values
    x["nxt"] = W.stack().reindex(pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([x.fm + 1, x.security_id])).values
    x = x.dropna()
    x["dec"] = x.groupby("fm").sig.transform(lambda s: pd.qcut(s.rank(method="first"), 10, labels=False) + 1)
    g = x.groupby(["fm", "dec"]).nxt.mean().unstack(); s = g[10] - g[1]
    rows.append((name, len(s), 100 * s.mean(), s.mean() / s.std() * np.sqrt(len(s))))
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["signal", "months", "D10 - D01 % a month", "t"]).round(2)

Average monthly turnover of the winners decile: 27.6%
Break-even cost: 4.19% of the value traded at each rebalance
Out[24]:
signal months D10 - D01 % a month t
0 12-0 (includes the last month) 190 2.37 4.46
1 12-1 (skips it) 190 2.32 4.49
2 1-0 (last month only) 196 0.52 1.30

Reading costs and the skipped month. The winners decile replaces about 28% of its names each month. Even so, it beats the NIFTY 500 unless trading costs exceed 4.2% of the value traded at every rebalance. Realistic costs for liquid NSE stocks (brokerage, securities transaction tax, impact) are a fraction of that, so costs alone cannot explain the premium away.

Skipping the most recent month, standard in US research because US stocks reverse over a month, makes no difference in India: 12-0 and 12-1 earn 2.37% and 2.32% a month. Last month's winners alone keep winning slightly (+0.52%, t = 1.3, not significant), where US data shows reversal. We keep 12-1 to stay comparable with published work.

3. What kinds of stocks are there? (k-means)¶

v_stock_features gives one row per stock in today's 500-stock universe with at least 48 of the last 60 full months: annualized return and volatility, beta, maximum drawdown, dividend yield (total minus price return), liquidity (log of average daily ₹ traded) and winner share (share of months in the top 3 momentum deciles).

Reading 3.1. Two pairs are strongly related: winner share and annual return (0.76), as expected, since five years of winning is a high return; and volatility and beta (0.61). Volatility and drawdown move together too (−0.54: more volatile, deeper falls). We keep all seven: each pair still carries a distinct shade (a stock can be volatile for its own reasons, with a low beta). Every feature is standardized first, so no feature dominates the distances because of its units.

3.2 Choosing k¶

Silhouette is highest at k = 2 (0.25), then roughly flat for k = 3–5 (0.21). The two-cluster split is just "the past five years' winners vs everything else". The elbow flattens after k = 4, and four clusters each have a clear financial meaning, so we choose k = 4 and test it in §3.3 with a variable the model never saw. The low silhouettes are themselves a finding: stock behaviour is a continuum, not a few tight types.

In [28]:

stk["distance"] = np.linalg.norm(X - km.cluster_centers_[km.labels_], axis=1)
centroids = stk.groupby("cluster")[FEATURES].mean()
centroids.assign(stocks=stk.groupby("cluster").size()).round(3)

# Name clusters by rules on the centroids, not by k-means' arbitrary label numbers
names, left = {}, set(centroids.index)
def take(col, how, name):
    sub = centroids.loc[sorted(left), col]
    c = sub.idxmax() if how == "max" else sub.idxmin()
    names[c] = name; left.discard(c)
take("winner_share", "max", "Momentum Leaders")
take("dividend_yield", "max", "Dividend Yielders")
take("ann_vol", "min", "Defensive Compounders")
take("ann_return", "min", "Volatile Laggards")
stk["segment"] = stk["cluster"].map(names)

3.3 Validation with a variable the model never saw: sector¶

The model saw only price behaviour, never the sector. If the segments are real economic groupings, sector membership should not be independent of segment. χ² test of independence on the sector × segment table (sectors with fewer than 10 stocks pooled).

In [33]:
sec = stk.sector.where(stk.sector.map(stk.sector.value_counts()) >= 10, "Other (small sectors)")
ct = pd.crosstab(sec, stk.segment)[list(DESC)]
chi2, p, dof, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(ct)
cramers_v = np.sqrt(chi2 / (ct.values.sum() * (min(ct.shape) - 1)))
print(f"chi2 = {chi2:.1f}, dof = {dof}, p = {p:.1e}, Cramér's V = {cramers_v:.2f}")
ct

chi2 = 228.2, dof = 42, p = 2.0e-27, Cramér's V = 0.43

Reading the validation. Sector, which the model never saw, is strongly associated with segment: χ² = 228 on 42 degrees of freedom, p ≈ 10⁻²⁷, Cramér's V = 0.43. Healthcare (21 of 30), FMCG (13 of 19) and Financial Services (40 of 68) are mostly Defensive Compounders; Capital Goods is split, but its largest group (26 of 48) is Momentum Leaders; Oil & Gas (8 of 14) and Metals (6 of 13) are mostly Dividend Yielders. Price behaviour alone recovers the economy's structure.

4. Write the segments back to the database¶

The labels go into segment and security_segment, so SQL can use them. This is the only step that connects as the owner, and it runs in one transaction: a failure leaves the old segments in place.

In [34]:
with writer.begin() as c:
    c.execute(text("DELETE FROM segment"))                # cascades to security_segment
    ids = {seg: c.execute(text("INSERT INTO segment (segment_name, description) VALUES (:n, :d) RETURNING segment_id"),
                          {"n": seg, "d": d}).scalar_one()
           for seg, d in DESC.items()}
    c.execute(text("INSERT INTO security_segment VALUES (:s, :g, :dist)"),
              [{"s": int(r.security_id), "g": ids[r.segment], "dist": round(float(r.distance), 3)}
               for r in stk.itertuples()])
query("SELECT segment_name, stocks, left(most_typical, 80) AS most_typical FROM v_segment_profile ORDER BY stocks DESC")

ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, ncol=2, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.1))
ax.set_title("Segment mix by sector (sectors ordered by size)")
save(fig, "09_sector_mix"); plt.show()

S1. WHICH SECTORS FALL INTO WHICH SEGMENT?

Reading S1. The chart shows the same thing per sector. The stocks not in today's NIFTY 500 list ("unclassified": liquid enough to rank in our top 500 but not index members) are almost all Momentum Leaders or Volatile Laggards (71 of 74): the edges of the market are where the extreme outcomes are.

Reading S2. In the market's down months (NIFTY 500 below −3%, average −5.2%), Defensive Compounders and Dividend Yielders fell least (−4.5%). Volatile Laggards fell hardest (−7.3%: 1.4× the market) and did not make it up in rallies (+7.5% against the market's +5.2%). Momentum Leaders fell slightly less than the market but rose more than twice as much (+12.3%) in up months.

The caveat matters: segments and S2 are measured on the same five years, so "Momentum Leaders rallied hardest" is partly true by construction. They are the stocks that went up. S2 describes how each kind of stock behaved; it is not evidence that the pattern will repeat.

6. Conclusions¶

How returns behave (§1). Single-stock returns have fat tails (excess kurtosis 7) and a positive skew; the index has a negative skew. Beta follows economics: construction, realty and power amplify the market, healthcare and FMCG damp it. Less traded stocks earned a little more, but not in a straight line.

Momentum (§2). Last year's winners beat last year's losers by 2.34% a month for 16 years (t = 4.5), the winners decile compounding at 26% a year against the index's 10%. The signal's rank correlation with next month's return (IC 0.06) is small but persistent. The database design is part of the result: a backtest on today's survivors would have added 2.4 points a year that never existed.

Why and when (§2.3). Four findings explain the premium:

  • It works only after rising markets: 3.13% a month after a rising year, nothing after a falling one, because bear markets end with the losers rebounding hardest.
  • It is not market risk: beta −0.51, alpha 2.80% a month (t = 5.7).
  • It is slow: the premium fades over 12 months without reversing, consistent with news reaching prices gradually.
  • It is shrinking: from 2.99% to 1.78% a month across the three sub-periods, still significant.

Two practical results follow. Sitting out after falling years raises the Sharpe ratio from 1.01 to 1.47 and halves the worst month (in-sample; untested out of sample). Trading costs would have to exceed 4.2% of the value traded to erase the premium.

Kinds of stock (§3–5). Four segments built only from price behaviour (Momentum Leaders, Defensive Compounders, Dividend Yielders, Volatile Laggards) line up with sectors the model never saw (Cramér's V 0.43). Defensive Compounders and Dividend Yielders lose least when the market falls; Volatile Laggards lose most and don't recover it.

Limitations.

  • Gross, price-only, equal-weighted returns; one flat cost assumption (0.5% per rebalance). Impact costs in the least liquid names would be higher.
  • Sectors exist only for today's NIFTY 500 members, so delisted and smaller stocks are "unclassified".
  • 82 price jumps around demergers and schemes of arrangement are set to 0 because NSE's notices give no ratio; a professional data vendor would adjust them.
  • Segments are descriptive: features and outcomes (S2) come from the same five years.
  • The market-state rule was chosen after seeing the data that tests it; its Sharpe ratio of 1.47 is in-sample.
